```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(clobe)
```

Many psychological theories make *ordinal* predictions: "people will respond
more to A than to B", "C and D will not differ". clobe therefore describes a
result not by its exact numbers but by its ordinal pattern: the relation
between every pair of conditions. This vignette explains how that pattern is
built and what kind of mathematical object it is.

## From numbers to an inequality matrix

Suppose a participant's results in $n$ conditions (stimuli) are
$v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$. For every pair of stimuli $i < j$ we record one of
three relations:

$$
m_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
\phantom{-}1 & \text{if } v_i - v_j > T \quad (i \text{ is larger than } j)\\
-1 & \text{if } v_i - v_j < -T \quad (i \text{ is smaller than } j)\\
\phantom{-}0 & \text{otherwise} \quad (i \text{ and } j \text{ are about the same})
\end{cases}
$$

$T$ is the **threshold**: the largest difference that we treat as no
difference at all. It should reflect how precisely the quantity is measured;
for example, a difference of one trial out of twenty is probably noise.

`imac()` (inequality matrix constructor) builds the matrix. The thresholds
are given as `c(upper, lower)`, normally `c(T, -T)`:

```{r}
imac(c(0.9, 0.5, 0.45, 0.1), thresholds = c(0.1, -0.1))
```

Read it row against column. Row 1, column 2 is `1`: stimulus 1 (0.9) is larger
than stimulus 2 (0.5). Row 2, column 3 is `0`: 0.5 and 0.45 are within 0.1 of
each other. The diagonal and everything below it are set to `2`, because they
repeat information already in the upper triangle (the relation of $j$ to $i$
is the opposite of $i$ to $j$). So a pattern over $n$ stimuli consists of
$n(n-1)/2$ relations, one per pair.

Two results have the **same pattern** if their upper triangles are equal,
even if their numbers differ:

```{r}
a <- imac(c(0.9, 0.5, 0.45, 0.1), c(0.1, -0.1))
b <- imac(c(0.8, 0.4, 0.42, 0.2), c(0.1, -0.1))
identical(a[upper.tri(a)], b[upper.tri(b)])
```

### A note on rounding

Computers store most decimals inexactly: `0.3 - 0.2` is not quite `0.1`.

```{r}
0.3 - 0.2 == 0.1
```

Without care, a difference that should sit exactly on the threshold could land
on either side of it depending on which numbers produced it. `imac()`
compares differences with a tiny tolerance (about $1.5 \times 10^{-8}$), so
equal steps are always treated alike.

## "About the same" is not transitive

The relation "is larger than" behaves as you would expect: if $a$ is larger
than $b$ and $b$ is larger than $c$, then $a$ is larger than $c$. "About the
same" does not. Here is a classic illustration (Luce, 1956): you cannot taste
the difference between a cup of coffee with 50 grains of sugar and one with
51, nor between 51 and 52, and so on, yet you can certainly taste the
difference between 50 and 100 grains.

The same happens with any threshold:

```{r}
imac(c(0.50, 0.58, 0.66), thresholds = c(0.1, -0.1))
```

Stimuli 1 and 2 are about the same (they differ by 0.08), as are 2 and 3, but
stimulus 1 is smaller than stimulus 3 (they differ by 0.16).

### Semiorders

A relation built this way, where $a$ counts as larger than $b$ only when it
exceeds $b$ by more than a fixed margin,

$$
a \succ b \iff u(a) > u(b) + T,
$$

is called a **semiorder** (Luce, 1956). Scott and Suppes (1958) showed that,
on a finite set, these are exactly the relations $\succ$ with three
properties:

1. Nothing is larger than itself.
2. If $a \succ b$ and $c \succ d$, then $a \succ d$ or $c \succ b$.
   *(Two clear differences cannot "cross" each other.)*
3. If $a \succ b$ and $b \succ c$, then for any other $d$, $a \succ d$ or
   $d \succ c$. *(A gap of two clear steps is too wide for anything to be
   about the same as both ends.)*

So every inequality matrix from `imac()` with symmetric thresholds is a
semiorder, and this is the default, `ordering = "semiorder"`. It is the right
choice when the threshold expresses measurement uncertainty, as it usually
does.

### Weak orderings

Sometimes we want "about the same" to mean "exactly tied". Then the relation
is a **weak ordering**: a ranking in which ties are allowed. Its tied groups
can be ranked from top to bottom, and "tied with" is transitive. With
`ordering = "weak"`, `imac()` ignores the thresholds and treats only exact
ties as equal:

```{r}
imac(c(0.50, 0.58, 0.66), thresholds = c(0.1, -0.1), ordering = "weak")
imac(c(0.50, 0.50, 0.66), thresholds = c(0.1, -0.1), ordering = "weak")
```

Formally, a weak ordering is a semiorder with $T = 0$:
$a \succ b \iff u(a) > u(b)$.

### What the difference looks like

Every weak ordering is a semiorder, but not the other way round. For three
stimuli there are 19 semiorders and 13 weak orderings. The 6 extra patterns
are exactly the "sugar in coffee" chains: two neighbours are each about the
same as the middle stimulus but clearly different from each other, in each of
the six ways of assigning stimuli to the three positions.

```{r}
key <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 3, function(m) paste(m[upper.tri(m)], collapse = ","))
}
semi <- orderings(3)$inequality_matrices
weak <- orderings(3, ordering = "weak")$inequality_matrices
extra <- semi[, , !(key(semi) %in% key(weak)), drop = FALSE]
dim(extra)[3]
extra[, , 1]
```

In this one, stimulus 3 is about the same as both 1 and 2, but 1 is smaller
than 2.

## Choosing the thresholds

- Use **symmetric** thresholds, `c(T, -T)`. With asymmetric thresholds,
  whether a pair counts as different depends on which stimulus comes first,
  which is rarely intended.
- Choose $T$ from how precisely the dependent variable is measured. For
  proportions from $N$ trials, one trial is a step of $1/N$.
- The patterns you can observe also depend on how finely the measurement
  scale is divided relative to $T$. `vignette("universal-set")` shows why
  this matters when counting the possible patterns.
